passage: At their school in Nagpur, a brown stray dog had started sleeping under the stairs, and the principal allowed it to stay if the eco-club looked after it. Payal, eleven, signed up for water duty before anyone else. Every morning she filled the steel bowl, checked it hadn't been knocked over at lunch, and wrote "done" on the chart by the staffroom. When Eshaan forgot his turn on Friday, she didn't complain to Ma'am. She just did it and reminded him, "Monday's yours, okay? She drinks a lot when it's hot." Eshaan nodded and wrote it on his hand.

qa.q: Where did the stray dog sleep?
qa.a: Under the stairs.

qa.q: Why didn't Payal complain to Ma'am when Eshaan forgot?
qa.a: She seemed to care more that the dog had water than about blaming anyone, and trusted a reminder would work.

qa.q: How could the eco-club make the duty easier to remember?
qa.a: Put up a simple rota everyone passes, or pair children so one can remind the other.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel after Payal quietly covers his turn?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed but grateful, and more likely to remember Monday because she didn't shame him.

grounding: It shows a girl taking active responsibility for a school animal and a group duty.

passage: I'm Bhupen, Leela's older brother. Since a new boy from Assam joined her Class 5, Leela has taken him on like a job. He doesn't speak much Hindi yet. I've seen her at the school gate drawing pictures in the dust to show which bus is his. At home she made him a list of useful words, "water," "toilet," "late," each with a drawing. When her friends went to play, she stayed back and ate lunch with him. I don't know if she likes him or if the teacher asked her. But she says "my buddy" in a very proud way.

qa.q: Which words did Leela put on the list?
qa.a: "Water," "toilet" and "late," each with a drawing.

qa.q: What does Leela saying "my buddy" in a proud way suggest?
qa.a: She seems to take real pride in the role and to care about helping him feel at home.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Leela so she doesn't carry it all?
qa.a: Add another buddy or two, so the new boy has more friends and Leela still gets time with her own.

qa.q: How might the new boy experience Leela's help?
qa.a: It probably makes a strange new school feel less lonely and confusing.

grounding: It shows, from a brother's view, a girl taking responsibility for helping a new classmate settle in.

passage:
Monday: Karthik, twelve, found a pigeon on the terrace that couldn't fly, one wing drooping. His sister Jyoti said, "Leave it, it'll die." He put it in a shoebox with a cloth and a bowl of water and asked Amma to call the animal helpline.
Wednesday: The volunteer had said to keep it quiet and warm until they could collect it. Karthik checked the box before and after school, speaking softly and not touching it.
Saturday: The volunteers came. Karthik carried the box down himself, then asked, "Do you need helpers on Sundays?" The next week, Jyoti went to the shelter with him.

qa.q: What did Karthik put the pigeon in?
qa.a: A shoebox with a cloth and a bowl of water.

qa.q: Why did Karthik ask about helping on Sundays?
qa.a: Caring for the pigeon made him want to keep helping animals, not just this one.

qa.q: Which of Karthik's choices kept the pigeon safest?
qa.a: Asking Amma to call the helpline and following the volunteer's advice to keep it quiet, instead of handling it himself.

qa.q: How did Jyoti's view change?
qa.a: She first said to leave it, but after seeing her brother's care she went to the shelter too. 🙂

grounding: It shows a boy taking active responsibility for an injured animal over a week and wanting to keep serving.

passage: Sit, beta, I'll tell you about your mother when she was ten. Shreya was the class monitor that year, and a thin brown dog used to sleep under the school stairs. Most children threw it a biscuit and forgot. Not Shreya. She made a chart on the back of her notebook: who brings the water bowl, who brings rotis, which day. Her friend Jaya took Tuesdays and Fridays. When the peon grumbled about the mess, Shreya and Jaya swept that corner themselves every evening before going home. By winter the dog followed the whole class to the gate. I still have that chart somewhere, folded in my cupboard.

qa.q: Where did the brown dog sleep?
qa.a: It slept under the school stairs.

qa.q: What does Shreya sweeping the corner herself suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt protective of the dog and saw it as her class's job, so rather than let the peon's complaint end the feeding, she fixed the mess herself.

qa.q: How could a teacher support children like Shreya who take on a job like this?
qa.a: A teacher could put the chart on the class wall and thank the helpers, so the duty is shared and does not all fall on one child.

qa.q: How might the peon have seen the dog feeding once the girls began sweeping?
qa.a: He probably found it less of a burden, since the mess was cleaned without him, and may have trusted the children more.

grounding: Illustrates a child taking steady responsibility for an animal and organising classmates into shared roles.

passage: The rain had been falling since lunch, and by four the school bus still had not come. Tanvir, eleven, had promised his teacher he would help Sarita this week, because her right arm was in a plaster and she could not carry her bag. Now the lane outside the gate was ankle-deep. He slung her bag across his chest over his own, took her umbrella in his free hand and held it over her cast instead of his head. 'Your shirt's soaked,' Sarita said. 'The plaster can't get wet. My shirt can,' he said. When the bus finally splashed up, he checked that she had a seat near the front before finding his own at the back, dripping and grinning.

qa.q: Why could Sarita not carry her own bag?
qa.a: Her right arm was in a plaster.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's reply about his shirt show about what he cared about most?
qa.a: It shows he cared more about keeping Sarita's plaster dry than about getting wet himself; he treated her comfort as his job that week. 🙂

qa.q: What small step could the school take so helpers like Tanvir are not stuck in the rain?
qa.a: The teacher could arrange a covered place to wait or a second helper, so the job stays safe and shared.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel about being helped this way?
qa.a: She might feel grateful and a little awkward, since she noticed he was getting soaked for her.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a peer-helper role he agreed to, even when heavy rain and a late bus make it harder.
